extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic and philosophy; people studying the nature and evaluation of syllogistic reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for understanding, constructing, and judging syllogisms and ratiocination: including the fundamental axioms (affirmative and negative), the proper provenance of inferences, and the role of general propositions, axioms, and diagrams in proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of affirmative syllogisms
rubrics_metrics.description: things which coexist with the same thing, coexist with one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as one of the fundamental axioms underlying all legitimate affirmative syllogistic inference; these axioms 'manifestly relate to facts, and not to conventions' and are the ground of the legitimacy of every argument in which facts (not conventions) are the matter treated of.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of negative syllogisms
rubrics_metrics.description: a thing which coexists with another thing, with which other a third thing does not coexist, is not coexistent with that third thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set out as the corresponding axiom for negative syllogisms; together with the affirmative axiom it forms the fundamental principles resembling mathematical axioms that justify syllogistic conclusions about factual matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark-phraseology general axiom
rubrics_metrics.description: whatever possesses any mark, possesses that which it is a mark of; or, whatever is a mark of any mark, is a mark of that which this last is a mark of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recommended reformulation of the two preceding axioms into a single, convenient phraseology. The author argues this wording is better adapted to express with precision what is accomplished in the ascertainment of truth by ratiocination, and shows how ordinary syllogisms translate into 'marks' language (e.g., attributes as marks of other attributes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogism validity condition (no more in conclusion than in premises)
rubrics_metrics.description: a syllogism is vicious if there be anything more in the conclusion than was assumed in the premisses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A classical criterion of validity: conclusions must not assert anything not already contained (explicitly or implicitly) in the premises. The text treats objections (petitio principii) and explores the apparent paradox that syllogisms seem to yield new knowledge while formally adding nothing beyond the premisses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference originates in particulars, not generals
rubrics_metrics.description: All inference is from particulars to particulars: General propositions are merely registers of such inferences already made, and short formulae for making more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General propositions are compressed records of observed cases plus the inferences drawn from them (induction). The 'major premiss' of a syllogism is a formula; the real logical antecedents are the particular facts from which that formula was induced. Evaluating an argument therefore requires checking the inductive basis in particulars, not treating the general premiss as the ultimate source of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between the inferring part and the registering part
rubrics_metrics.description: the distinction between the inferring part, and the registering part; ascribing to the latter the functions of the former is error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained with examples (e.g., the Duke of Wellington case): when a person cites a general premiss they are often 'reading' a memorandum of past induction rather than performing the original inference at that moment. Critics who treat the register (general statement) as the origin of knowledge mistake the real epistemic process; in assessing reasoning one should seek the original inductive grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of the syllogism as precautions to ensure correct reading
rubrics_metrics.description: the rules of the syllogism are a set of precautions to ensure our doing so [reading the record correctly].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practical function of syllogistic rules is to prevent misreading or misapplying the evidential record (the general formula that encodes past particulars). Especially when the original particulars are forgotten, syllogistic rules help ensure that conclusions drawn according to the formula indeed correspond to the facts on which the formula was based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy and ubiquity of reasoning from particulars to particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: We may reason from particulars to particulars, without passing through generals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that much human (and animal) reasoning operates directly from remembered particulars to new particulars (e.g., a child avoiding fire after being burnt) without explicit generalization. Evaluating practical reasoning should acknowledge that direct particular-to-particular inference is valid and often primary; general propositions are a later convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of axioms and definitions in proofs (general statements as shorthand)
rubrics_metrics.description: the general propositions, whether called definitions, axioms, or laws of nature, which we lay down at the beginning of our reasonings, are merely abridged statements in a kind of short hand, of the particular facts, which... we either think we may proceed upon as proved, or intend to assume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mathematical and geometrical demonstrations one often proves a single particular case via a diagram; the general theorem is then a shorthand indicating that the same mode of proof applies to all similar cases. Axioms/definitions are necessary assumptions and useful for concision, but proofs fundamentally rest on particular assumptions (specimens) and on the ability to recognize similar configurations.
